question: Assume the JTB definition of Knowledge, which suggests that "Knowledge is a Justified True Belief". If our only available epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief, what are the two problems JTB runs into? Ignore Gettier problems.

1.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two problems are (1) the regress of justification and (2) the foundationalist dilemma. Under JTB, a belief counts as knowledge only if it is justified. But if the only epistemic states available are Knowledge and Belief, then any justifier must itself be either a further belief or a piece of knowledge. Since knowledge entails belief, even an appeal to knowledge still leaves us with a belief-state whose justification can be challenged. So justification either continues indefinitely, producing an endless chain of justifiers, or we must stop the chain by treating some belief as basic. But that stopping point cannot itself be justified without restarting the regress; it is either unjustified or self-justifying, making the foundation arbitrary or vacuous. Thus JTB faces the regress problem and the problem of arbitrary foundations.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two problems are (1) the infinite regress of justification and (2) the arbitrary-foundation problem. On JTB, a belief counts as knowledge only if it is justified. But if the justification must itself be known or further justified, then justifying any one belief requires another justified belief, which requires another, and so on—an infinite regress. To stop the regress, one might appeal to a basic belief accepted without further justification. But since our only epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief, such a stopping point can only be a mere Belief, not Knowledge. That makes the whole justificatory structure rest on an arbitrary, unjustified belief, so JTB either never gets off the ground or collapses into unjustified belief.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Under JTB Knowledge = Justified + True + Belief. If Knowledge and Belief are the only two epistemic kinds that are available then everything that is not JTB must be called Belief.

That makes Belief a disjunctive / heterogeneous catch-all.

* Justified false belief. It is justified, hence it is epistemically good in the way justification is, but it is false so by JTB it is not Knowledge. With only Knowledge / Belief as options it has to be classified as mere Belief, i.e. as the same kind of state as an unjustified false belief. The epistemic value of the justification is therefore lost in the label ‘Belief’.

* True belief without justification. It is true, hence it is epistemically good in the way truth is, but it is unjustified so by JTB it is not Knowledge. With only Knowledge / Belief as options it has to be classified as mere Belief, i.e. as the same kind of state as a justified false belief. The epistemic value of the truth is therefore lost in the label ‘Belief’.

Hence on a strict JTB taxonomy Belief = justified false belief ∨ unjustified true belief ∨ unjustified false belief. The state ‘justified belief’ strictly speaking, and the state ‘true belief’ strictly speaking, have no place in the taxonomy. Knowledge is made the only positive state and Belief becomes the name for two importantly different kinds of epistemic failure – failure of truth vs failure of justification – and for their conjunction. That is why the standard taxonomy is normally expanded to at least Justified Belief and True Belief as intermediate, non-knowledge states.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two problems are the infinite regress of justification and the basing-relation problem. On JTB, knowledge requires a justified belief. But if the only epistemic states available are knowledge and belief, then the justifier must itself be either known or believed. If it is known, then it needs its own justification, and the chain never terminates—this is the infinite regress. If it is merely believed, then the original belief may be true and accompanied by a justifying belief, but JTB does not explain why the belief is actually based on that justification rather than merely coinciding with it. Since the basing relation is neither a case of knowledge nor a case of belief, JTB cannot account for it using only those two states. So the two problems are infinite regress and the basing relation.

2.text:
Under the JTB analysis S knows that p iff

* S believes that p,
* p is true,
* S is justified in believing that p.

If Knowledge and Belief are the **only** epistemic kinds there is in the
order, then the third condition can only be satisfied by something which
is itself a Knowledge or a Belief. Knowledge is belief plus truth plus
justification, so for expository purposes the justifying condition has to
come from a belief.

So a belief is knowledge just in case it is true and it is supported by
another belief, and that supporting belief is itself true and supported,
etc. There is no intermediate standing such as ‘justified belief’ or
‘well-founded belief’ which is distinct from knowledge.

That forces two well known difficulties. 

* Regulative circularity / regress. If the justifier for p is a mere
belief q, q can be justified only by a further belief r, r only by s,
and so on.  You get the classic Agrippa trilemma: an infinite regress of
beliefs justifying beliefs, a vicious circle of beliefs justifying each
other, or a dogmatic stopping point where a belief is taken as
justified while being only a belief. On a strict Knowledge/Belief
taxonomy there is no third, non-epistemic stopping place for
justification. In particular, if you insist that a justifier be
knowledge, knowledge requires justification which requires knowledge,
so knowledge can only be grounded in antecedent knowledge.

* Collapse of the epistemic taxonomy. With only Belief < Knowledge,
every belief which is not knowledge is just “belief”.  Hence

JFB – a justified false belief – and UTB – an unjustified true belief –
are both lumped together with plain unjustified false belief as mere
belief.  Justified false belief is epistemically good in the ordinary
sense of being responsibly held, yet by JTB it is not knowledge because
it is false, and it has no distinct epistemic standing at all.  Unjustified
true belief is epistemically defective, yet by JTB it is indistinguishable
from a justified false belief: both are just beliefs that are not
knowledge.  So JTB, on a two-state taxonomy, cannot mark the normative
difference between being right for the right reasons, being right by
accident, and being wrong for the right reasons.

Those are the familiar non-Gettier costs of trying to build justification
out of belief and knowledge alone.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two problems are: (1) the infinite regress of justification—if the justification for a belief must itself be a further belief, then every justified belief needs another justified belief, with no non-arbitrary stopping point within the K/B framework; and (2) the access/factivity problem—truth is not an epistemic state, so JTB cannot explain how a subject can distinguish knowledge from mere belief from the inside. Gettier cases aside, these are structural difficulties the definition faces.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two problems are (1) the infinite regress of justification and (2) the problem of arbitrary or dogmatic termination. JTB says a belief counts as knowledge only if it is justified. But justification for a belief normally comes from another belief. If every justifying belief must itself be justified, the chain of reasons cannot end without either going on forever—an infinite regress—or stopping at some belief that is accepted without further justification. That stopping point is dogmatic or arbitrary, and JTB cannot allow it because the belief is not justified. So JTB is caught between an unending regress and an unjustified foundation.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: On the JTB tripartite analysis Knowledge = Belief & True & Justified so justification and truth are two independent dimensions. With a justification x truth matrix there are in principle four epistemic cells

* J T = justified true belief = Knowledge on JTB
* J F = justified false belief
* U T = unjustified true belief
* U F = unjustified false belief

If the only tags you are allowed to use for an attitude are ‘Knowledge’ and unqualified ‘Belief’, the J T cell is the only one that can be marked off as distinct. Every other combination is forced into the undifferentiated Belief bucket. 

That means the Belief bucket has to do the work of two qualitatively different cases.

1. Justified false belief. A belief can be epistemically good, well supported, in fact justified, and still be false. On JTB it is not Knowledge because it is not true, so it must be classified as Belief. With only Knowledge/Belief there is no way to mark the normative difference between a justified false belief and an unjustified false belief. Justification is invisible inside Belief.

2. Unjustified true belief. A belief can be true by luck, accident or sheer coincidence and be epistemically worthless because it is unjustified. On JTB it is not Knowledge because it is not justified, so it must be classified as Belief. With only Knowledge/Belief there is no way to mark the normative difference between an unjustified true belief and a justified true belief that fails to be Knowledge for other reasons. Truth without justification is invisible inside Belief.

Hence justification and truth are both lost as independent markers of epistemic value once every non-K case is lumped together as mere Belief. That is the classic under-determination of the two-by-two justification × truth space by a two-state taxonomy, and it is why an adequate taxonomy needs at least the J F and U T cells in addition to Knowledge. Gettier aside, that is the collapse of the justified/false and true/unjustified distinctions into an undifferentiated Belief category.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: The two problems are (1) the infinite regress of justification and (2) the arbitrariness of any foundational stopping point. On JTB, a belief only qualifies as knowledge if it is justified. But if justification must itself be an epistemic state, then a justifying belief either needs a further justification—leading to an endless regress—or, if we halt the chain with a basic belief, that basic belief is not justified by anything further. Under JTB, such a stopping point is merely a belief, not knowledge, so it cannot non-arbitrarily ground the knowledge claim. Thus JTB either never completes the justification or must rely on an unjustified foundation. (Setting aside Gettier cases.)

11.text:
With a binary taxonomy Knowledge / Belief you can only mark the three-place
conjunction J & T & B as Knowledge and everything else as mere Belief.
That collapses the 2 x 2 x 2 space of justification × truth × belief into
two cells and you lose two epistemically distinct non-knowledge positions.

* Justified non-knowledge. J & B & ~T
A justified false belief is rationally held, in the sense that the subject
has good reasons for it, and yet it is not Knowledge because ~T. On a
Knowledge/Belief dichotomy it has to be classed as mere Belief, and it is
therefore lumped together with unjustified false beliefs, irrational false
beliefs, etc. You need a distinct state, justified belief, to mark the
epistemic value of being justified even when the belief turns out false.

* True non-knowledge. T & B & ~J
An unjustified true belief is true and believed but held on no good
grounds, a lucky guess. It is not Knowledge because ~J. On a
Knowledge/Belief dichotomy it has to be classed as mere Belief, and it is
therefore lumped together with justified false beliefs and with false
beliefs generally. You need a distinct state, true belief / accidental
belief, to mark the epistemic difference between a true belief that is
held for a reason and a true belief that is merely lucky.

In other words the JTB analysis forces you to treat

JFB = justified false belief  and  UTB = unjustified true belief

as the same undifferentiated “Belief” state, whereas epistemically
JFB is a rational error and UTB is a lucky hit, both different from an
ordinary unjustified false belief. That is why the classic analysis is
usually expanded to at least four states: Knowledge = JTB, Justified
Belief = JB, True Belief = TB, and mere Belief.

6.text:
Under the JTB analysis
K p  <=>  B p  &  T p  &  J p
the justification condition is supposed to do the normative work. If
the only doxastic attitudes you are allowed to talk about are B and K
then J p cannot be a third attitude. It has to be reconstrued as B q or
K q for some q that is supposed to support p.

If J p is reconstrued as belief, K p requires a further belief q that
supports p and is itself believed. To be a genuine justifier q has to
be justified as well, so you need a belief r that supports q, and so on.
That is the familiar regress of the justifiers:

B p justified by B q justified by B r ...

With only B and K in the inventory the regress can never stop in a
justified basic belief, because a basic belief would be a belief that
is justified without being believed to be justified. The only stopping
points you have are

* B, an unjustified belief, which is not knowledge, or
* K, a belief that is already itself justified.

If you stop in K you get the second structure. Let J p be K q. Then

K p  ->  K q  &  B p & T p

and q is a proposition that is supposed to make p justified. In the
normal case q is about p or about the grounds for p, so the justification
of p is itself a piece of knowledge about p. You get

K p  ->  K p

or at best a closed justificatory circle. Knowledge of p is made to
depend on knowledge of the justification for p which already presupposes
knowledge of p. The only alternatives are an endless hierarchy of
higher order beliefs or a vicious circle.

That structural collapse is visible in the doxastic space you are left
with. With only K and B the four combinations of truth value and
justification collapse to two cells:

* T & J  =  K
* ¬T & J , ¬T & ¬J , T & ¬J  =  B

So a justified false belief and an unjustified false belief are
indistinguishable in the inventory; they are both just 'belief'. The
normative difference between a rationally held false belief and an
irrationally held false belief is lost. Likewise an unjustified true
belief, e.g. a lucky guess, and a justified false belief are both
classified only as belief, so the epistemic defect of belief by luck
and the epistemic virtue of being justified but unlucky are
indistinguishable. In ordinary talk we want to be able to say that a
justified false belief is epistemically good in the sense of being
responsible, and that an unjustified true belief is epistemically bad
in the sense of being lucky, while neither is knowledge. JTB with a
B/K inventory cannot mark that distinction; justification cannot be
made a distinct epistemic state without either an infinite regress of
justifying beliefs or a circular self-justification of knowledge.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With JTB Knowledge = Believe & Justified & True, Belief = not Knowledge has to do the work for the three remaining truth-justification combinations.

On a JTB picture a subject can be in at least four distinct doxastic positions wrt p:

* JTB = Knowledge
* J & B & not T = a justified false belief
* not J & B & T = a true but unjustified belief
* not J & B & not T = an unjustified false belief

If the only epistemic predicates you are allowed to use are Knowledge and Belief, the last three positions all have to be called ‘Belief’. That makes Belief an heterogeneous, unprincipled class.

In particular:

1. Justification without truth. JTB entails the existence of justified false beliefs. A justified false belief is not Knowledge because it is not true, but it is epistemically good in the sense of being justified. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it has to be classified as mere Belief, and so justified false belief is lumped together with unjustified false belief and with true but unjustified belief. You lose the ability to mark justification as an independent epistemic value.

2. Truth without justification. JTB entails the existence of true beliefs that are not justified. A true but unjustified belief is not Knowledge because it is not justified, but it is true. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it likewise has to be classified as mere Belief, so a true but unjustified belief is lumped together with false beliefs and with justified false beliefs. You lose the ability to mark truth as an independent epistemic value.

Hence a binary Knowledge vs Belief taxonomy forces the conflation of justified false belief with unjustified belief, and of unjustified true belief with false belief. JTB needs at least the distinct categories of justified belief and of true belief in order to keep justification and truth separately trackable; with only Knowledge and Belief you cannot. That is the pre-Gettier cost of reducing knowledge to just a species of belief.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: On the JTB picture knowledge is true belief + justification. If the only
attitudes you are allowed to ascribe to a subject are *knows that p* and *believes that p*,
justification has no independent attitude-status, it is collapsed into the
knowledge/belief distinction. That collapses the normal 2 × 2 × 2 logical space of
truth / belief / justification into two cells and you lose two intuitively
distinct intermediate doxastic statuses.

1. Justified false belief. Justification does not entail truth. There are
intuitively justified but false beliefs, e.g. a belief formed on the best
available evidence at the time that turns out false, or a well-supported
scientific belief that is later refuted. On JTB that state is not knowledge
because truth fails, and with only Knowledge and Belief as options it is
forced to be mere belief. The epistemic value conferred by justification is
therefore lost: a justified false belief is epistemically better than an
unjustified false belief, but the taxonomy cannot mark the difference.

In the limit, if belief is taken to be the state that is left when
knowledge is removed, belief becomes by definition unjustified, so a
justified false belief becomes impossible on the taxonomy. JTB therefore
rules out the very plausible category of a justified but false belief,
or else it must call it knowledge, which is false.

2. True belief without justification. Truth does not entail justification.
There are intuitively true but unjustified beliefs, e.g. a lucky guess,
a correct belief formed by wishful thinking, or a true belief whose
justifying grounds are missing. On JTB that state is not knowledge because
justification fails, and with only Knowledge and Belief as options it is
forced to be mere belief. The difference between a justified true belief
which by JTB is knowledge and an unjustified true belief which is merely
lucky is therefore unmarked. You cannot distinguish a lucky true belief
from a justified true belief, and you cannot distinguish an unjustified true
belief from an unjustified false belief, because both are just ‘belief’.

Hence with a binary knowledge/belief ontology JTB either over-intellectualises
belief by making any justified belief knowledge whenever it happens to be
true, and it under-intellectualises belief by making all false beliefs,
justified or not, mere belief. The classic intermediate cases of justified
false belief and unjustified true belief have no home, which is the taxonomic
price of reducing justification to the knowledge/belief divide. This is
distinct from the Gettier problem, which is about justified true belief that
is still not knowledge.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With only the two doxastic kinds Knowledge and Mere Belief there is no box for
the two mixed T/F x J/UJ cases that JTB forces into the single box 'Belief'.

On the JTB scheme Knowledge = T & J & B.  So:

* T & J & B = Knowledge
* ¬T & J & B, ¬T & ¬J & B, T & ¬J & B are all just Belief.

Hence the taxonomy collapses justification for the false case and truth for the
non-knowledge case.

1. The justified false belief problem. A belief can be epistemically good by being
justified while being false. On JTB with only Knowledge/Belief a justified false
belief is not Knowledge because ¬T, and it is not a distinct state at all: it is
simply classified as Belief. The same Belief box is then also occupied by an
unjustified false belief. Justification is therefore invisible in the false
domain; a carefully justified error is epistemically indistinguishable from a
random false belief.

2. The unjustified / lucky true belief problem. A true belief can be epistemically
bad by being true only by luck/accident, ¬J. On JTB that belief is not Knowledge
because ¬J, and with only Knowledge/Belief it is simply classified as Belief.
The same Belief box is then also occupied by any false belief, justified or not.
Truth is therefore invisible in the non-knowledge domain; a lucky true belief is
epistemically indistinguishable from a false belief.

In effect JTB can only register justification when truth is present and can
only register truth when justification is present. Justified false belief and
unjustified true belief have no distinct epistemic place and are both
downgraded to unqualified Belief.

If J p is reconstrued as belief, K p requires a further belief q that
supports p and is itself believed. To be a genuine justifier q has to
be justified as well, so you need a belief r that supports q, and so on.
That is the familiar regress of the justifiers:

B p justified by B q justified by B r ...

With only B and K in the inventory the regress can never stop in a
justified basic belief, because a basic belief would be a belief that
is justified without being believed to be justified. The only stopping
points you have are

* B, an unjustified belief, which is not knowledge, or
* K, a belief that is already itself justified.

If you stop in K you get the second structure. Let J p be K q. Then

K p  ->  K q  &  B p & T p

and q is a proposition that is supposed to make p justified. In the
normal case q is about p or about the grounds for p, so the justification
of p is itself a piece of knowledge about p. You get

K p  ->  K p

or at best a closed justificatory circle. Knowledge of p is made to
depend on knowledge of the justification for p which already presupposes
knowledge of p. The only alternatives are an endless hierarchy of
higher order beliefs or a vicious circle.

That structural collapse is visible in the doxastic space you are left
with. With only K and B the four combinations of truth value and
justification collapse to two cells:

* T & J  =  K
* ¬T & J , ¬T & ¬J , T & ¬J  =  B

So a justified false belief and an unjustified false belief are
indistinguishable in the inventory; they are both just 'belief'. The
normative difference between a rationally held false belief and an
irrationally held false belief is lost. Likewise an unjustified true
belief, e.g. a lucky guess, and a justified false belief are both
classified only as belief, so the epistemic defect of belief by luck
and the epistemic virtue of being justified but unlucky are
indistinguishable. In ordinary talk we want to be able to say that a
justified false belief is epistemically good in the sense of being
responsible, and that an unjustified true belief is epistemically bad
in the sense of being lucky, while neither is knowledge. JTB with a
B/K inventory cannot mark that distinction; justification cannot be
made a distinct epistemic state without either an infinite regress of
justifying beliefs or a circular self-justification of knowledge.
public_text.10:
With JTB Knowledge = Believe & Justified & True, Belief = not Knowledge has to do the work for the three remaining truth-justification combinations.

On a JTB picture a subject can be in at least four distinct doxastic positions wrt p:

* JTB = Knowledge
* J & B & not T = a justified false belief
* not J & B & T = a true but unjustified belief
* not J & B & not T = an unjustified false belief

If the only epistemic predicates you are allowed to use are Knowledge and Belief, the last three positions all have to be called ‘Belief’. That makes Belief an heterogeneous, unprincipled class.

In particular:

1. Justification without truth. JTB entails the existence of justified false beliefs. A justified false belief is not Knowledge because it is not true, but it is epistemically good in the sense of being justified. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it has to be classified as mere Belief, and so justified false belief is lumped together with unjustified false belief and with true but unjustified belief. You lose the ability to mark justification as an independent epistemic value.

2. Truth without justification. JTB entails the existence of true beliefs that are not justified. A true but unjustified belief is not Knowledge because it is not justified, but it is true. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it likewise has to be classified as mere Belief, so a true but unjustified belief is lumped together with false beliefs and with justified false beliefs. You lose the ability to mark truth as an independent epistemic value.

Hence a binary Knowledge vs Belief taxonomy forces the conflation of justified false belief with unjustified belief, and of unjustified true belief with false belief. JTB needs at least the distinct categories of justified belief and of true belief in order to keep justification and truth separately trackable; with only Knowledge and Belief you cannot. That is the pre-Gettier cost of reducing knowledge to just a species of belief.
public_text.12:
On the JTB picture knowledge is true belief + justification. If the only
attitudes you are allowed to ascribe to a subject are *knows that p* and *believes that p*,
justification has no independent attitude-status, it is collapsed into the
knowledge/belief distinction. That collapses the normal 2 × 2 × 2 logical space of
truth / belief / justification into two cells and you lose two intuitively
distinct intermediate doxastic statuses.

1. Justified false belief. Justification does not entail truth. There are
intuitively justified but false beliefs, e.g. a belief formed on the best
available evidence at the time that turns out false, or a well-supported
scientific belief that is later refuted. On JTB that state is not knowledge
because truth fails, and with only Knowledge and Belief as options it is
forced to be mere belief. The epistemic value conferred by justification is
therefore lost: a justified false belief is epistemically better than an
unjustified false belief, but the taxonomy cannot mark the difference.

In the limit, if belief is taken to be the state that is left when
knowledge is removed, belief becomes by definition unjustified, so a
justified false belief becomes impossible on the taxonomy. JTB therefore
rules out the very plausible category of a justified but false belief,
or else it must call it knowledge, which is false.

2. True belief without justification. Truth does not entail justification.
There are intuitively true but unjustified beliefs, e.g. a lucky guess,
a correct belief formed by wishful thinking, or a true belief whose
justifying grounds are missing. On JTB that state is not knowledge because
justification fails, and with only Knowledge and Belief as options it is
forced to be mere belief. The difference between a justified true belief
which by JTB is knowledge and an unjustified true belief which is merely
lucky is therefore unmarked. You cannot distinguish a lucky true belief
from a justified true belief, and you cannot distinguish an unjustified true
belief from an unjustified false belief, because both are just ‘belief’.

Hence with a binary knowledge/belief ontology JTB either over-intellectualises
belief by making any justified belief knowledge whenever it happens to be
true, and it under-intellectualises belief by making all false beliefs,
justified or not, mere belief. The classic intermediate cases of justified
false belief and unjustified true belief have no home, which is the taxonomic
price of reducing justification to the knowledge/belief divide. This is
distinct from the Gettier problem, which is about justified true belief that
is still not knowledge.
public_text.8:
With only the two doxastic kinds Knowledge and Mere Belief there is no box for
the two mixed T/F x J/UJ cases that JTB forces into the single box 'Belief'.

On the JTB scheme Knowledge = T & J & B.  So:

* T & J & B = Knowledge
* ¬T & J & B, ¬T & ¬J & B, T & ¬J & B are all just Belief.

Hence the taxonomy collapses justification for the false case and truth for the
non-knowledge case.

1. The justified false belief problem. A belief can be epistemically good by being
justified while being false. On JTB with only Knowledge/Belief a justified false
belief is not Knowledge because ¬T, and it is not a distinct state at all: it is
simply classified as Belief. The same Belief box is then also occupied by an
unjustified false belief. Justification is therefore invisible in the false
domain; a carefully justified error is epistemically indistinguishable from a
random false belief.

2. The unjustified / lucky true belief problem. A true belief can be epistemically
bad by being true only by luck/accident, ¬J. On JTB that belief is not Knowledge
because ¬J, and with only Knowledge/Belief it is simply classified as Belief.
The same Belief box is then also occupied by any false belief, justified or not.
Truth is therefore invisible in the non-knowledge domain; a lucky true belief is
epistemically indistinguishable from a false belief.

In effect JTB can only register justification when truth is present and can
only register truth when justification is present. Justified false belief and
unjustified true belief have no distinct epistemic place and are both
downgraded to unqualified Belief.

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about the cost of a strict Knowledge / Belief binary under JTB = Justified & True & Belief, Gettier set aside.

The dominant thread in round 0 is taxonomic collapse. With JTB, the 2×2 justification × truth space is:

* J & T & B = Knowledge
* J & ~T & B = justified false belief
* ~J & T & B = unjustified true belief / lucky true belief
* ~J & ~T & B = unjustified false belief

If the only predicates allowed are Knowledge and unqualified Belief, the first cell is Knowledge and the remaining three cells are all forced into the single label ‘Belief’. Belief therefore becomes a heterogeneous catch-all.

That yields two distinct losses:

1. Justification without truth is unmarked. A justified false belief is epistemically good in being responsibly held, but ~T so it is not Knowledge by JTB. On a K/B only taxonomy it is classed as mere Belief and is indistinguishable from an unjustified false belief. Justification is invisible in the false domain; you cannot mark the normative difference between a rational error and an irrational error.

2. Truth without justification is unmarked. An unjustified true belief is true but held by luck/accident, ~J so it is not Knowledge by JTB. On a K/B only taxonomy it is also classed as mere Belief and is indistinguishable from justified false beliefs and from false beliefs generally. Truth is invisible in the non-knowledge domain; you cannot mark the normative difference between a lucky hit and a justified error, nor between a lucky true belief and a false belief.

Hence JTB needs distinct intermediate states – justified belief and true belief – to keep justification and truth trackable independently of their conjunction. With only K/B, justification only “counts” when truth is present and truth only “counts” when justification is present.

Note disagreement in the room. A minority strand, Colleague 1,13,14,9 and partly 2,5,6,7, argues the core difficulty is structural/regulative: if justification can only be carried by a Knowledge or a Belief, a justifier for p must itself be justified, leading to infinite regress, vicious circularity, or a dogmatic foundational stopping point that is merely Belief and therefore not knowledge. That is the Agrippa trilemma / arbitrary foundation problem. Colleague 2 and 6 present both the regress/circularity and the taxonomic collapse together.

Unresolved: whether the question is intended as the purely classificatory problems of justified false belief and unjustified true belief, or as regress + foundation. The binary-state constraint most directly licenses the classificatory collapse, which is why most colleagues frame the two problems as the justified-false and the unjustified-true cases. Gettier is explicitly excluded.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The discussion is split on which two non-Gettier costs are most salient under the constraint “only Knowledge and Belief are available”.

The dominant taxonomy-collapse strand, Colleagues 10,11,12,3,4,6,8 and in part Colleague 2, notes JTB = B & T & J. With J × T there are four cells:
* J T = Knowledge
* J ¬T = justified false belief
* ¬J T = unjustified true / lucky true belief
* ¬J ¬T = unjustified false belief

If the only predicates allowed are Knowledge vs unqualified Belief, the J T cell is the only one that can be marked off. J ¬T, ¬J T and ¬J ¬T all have to be called mere Belief. That makes Belief heterogeneous.

1. Justification without truth is lost. A justified false belief is epistemically good in the sense of being responsibly held, but not Knowledge because ¬T. On a binary taxonomy it must be called Belief and is lumped with unjustified false belief. Justification becomes invisible in the false domain; we cannot mark the normative difference between a rational error and an irrational error.

2. Truth without justification is lost. An unjustified true belief is true but held by luck/accident, not Knowledge because ¬J. On a binary taxonomy it must be called Belief and is lumped with justified false belief and with plain false belief. Truth becomes invisible in the non-knowledge domain; a lucky hit is epistemically indistinguishable from a false belief.

Hence JTB needs distinct intermediate states – justified belief and true belief – to keep justification and truth separately trackable. With only Knowledge/Belief the 2×2 J×T space collapses to two cells.

A second strand, Colleagues 1,13,14,9,5,7, and partly Colleague 2 and 6, frames the cost as justificatory regress / foundation. Because justification must be realized by a further epistemic state, on a Knowledge/Belief only inventory it must be a further belief or a piece of knowledge. Knowledge already requires justification, so a justifier that is knowledge reintroduces the same requirement. This yields Agrippa’s trilemma: infinite regress of justifiers Bq, Br, …; vicious circularity; or a dogmatic stopping point. A basic belief would be a Belief not justified by anything further, i.e. not Knowledge, so the chain rests on an arbitrary/unjustified foundation. Colleague 5 adds the basing-relation problem: JTB cannot explain why the belief is based on its justifier rather than merely coinciding with it using only K/B.

The two strands overlap: the regress/foundation worry is why a binary inventory cannot give justification an independent standing; the taxonomy worry is the observable consequence that JFB and UTB have no home and are conflated under mere Belief. The question explicitly limits epistemic states to Knowledge and Belief and asks to ignore Gettier, which points to the collapse of JFB and UTB as the direct binary-taxonomy problems, while regress/foundation is the classic structural cost of building justification out of belief/knowledge alone. Unresolved is whether the intended “two problems” are the two collapsed cells or regress + arbitrary foundation.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The JTB analysis is K p ≡ B p ∧ T p ∧ J p. With only the two doxastic labels Knowledge and unqualified Belief there is no independent attitude for justification or for truth. The 2×2 justification × truth space therefore collapses to two cells:

* J ∧ T ∧ B = Knowledge
* ¬J ∧ T ∧ B , J ∧ ¬T ∧ B , ¬J ∧ ¬T ∧ B = all labelled Belief

That collapse is the core non-Gettier cost.

Two distinct non-knowledge positions are thereby lost inside the undifferentiated Belief bucket:

1. Justification without truth – justified false belief, J ∧ B ∧ ¬T. It is epistemically good in the sense of being responsibly held, but it is not Knowledge because ¬T. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it must be called mere Belief and is lumped together with unjustified false belief. 2. Truth without justification – unjustified true belief, T ∧ B ∧ ¬J. It is true but held by luck/accident and is not Knowledge because ¬J. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it must also be called mere Belief and is lumped together with justified false belief and unjustified false belief. Truth becomes invisible in the non-knowledge domain; a lucky hit cannot be distinguished from a false belief.

Colleague 5 additionally notes the basing-relation problem; colleague 7 notes an access/factivity worry.

I am keeping both descriptions in mind: the taxonomy collapse into JFB and UTB as the explicit two-cell loss, and the regress/arbitrary foundation formulation as the dynamic consequence of having to build justification out of only K and B. reflection_text.2:
The question is about the cost of a strict Knowledge / Belief binary under JTB = Justified & True & Belief, Gettier set aside.

The dominant thread in round 0 is taxonomic collapse. With JTB, the 2×2 justification × truth space is:

* J & T & B = Knowledge
* J & ~T & B = justified false belief
* ~J & T & B = unjustified true belief / lucky true belief
* ~J & ~T & B = unjustified false belief

If the only predicates allowed are Knowledge and unqualified Belief, the first cell is Knowledge and the remaining three cells are all forced into the single label ‘Belief’. Belief therefore becomes a heterogeneous catch-all.

That yields two distinct losses:

1. Justification without truth is unmarked. A justified false belief is epistemically good in being responsibly held, but ~T so it is not Knowledge by JTB. On a K/B only taxonomy it is classed as mere Belief and is indistinguishable from an unjustified false belief. Justification is invisible in the false domain; you cannot mark the normative difference between a rational error and an irrational error.

2. Truth without justification is unmarked. An unjustified true belief is true but held by luck/accident, ~J so it is not Knowledge by JTB. On a K/B only taxonomy it is also classed as mere Belief and is indistinguishable from justified false beliefs and from false beliefs generally. Truth is invisible in the non-knowledge domain; you cannot mark the normative difference between a lucky hit and a justified error, nor between a lucky true belief and a false belief.

Hence JTB needs distinct intermediate states – justified belief and true belief – to keep justification and truth trackable independently of their conjunction. With only K/B, justification only “counts” when truth is present and truth only “counts” when justification is present.

Note disagreement in the room. A minority strand, Colleague 1,13,14,9 and partly 2,5,6,7, argues the core difficulty is structural/regulative: if justification can only be carried by a Knowledge or a Belief, a justifier for p must itself be justified, leading to infinite regress, vicious circularity, or a dogmatic foundational stopping point that is merely Belief and therefore not knowledge. That is the Agrippa trilemma / arbitrary foundation problem. Colleague 2 and 6 present both the regress/circularity and the taxonomic collapse together.

Unresolved: whether the question is intended as the purely classificatory problems of justified false belief and unjustified true belief, or as regress + foundation. The binary-state constraint most directly licenses the classificatory collapse, which is why most colleagues frame the two problems as the justified-false and the unjustified-true cases. Gettier is explicitly excluded.
reflection_text.3:
The discussion is split on which two non-Gettier costs are most salient under the constraint “only Knowledge and Belief are available”.

The dominant taxonomy-collapse strand, Colleagues 10,11,12,3,4,6,8 and in part Colleague 2, notes JTB = B & T & J. With J × T there are four cells:
* J T = Knowledge
* J ¬T = justified false belief
* ¬J T = unjustified true / lucky true belief
* ¬J ¬T = unjustified false belief

If the only predicates allowed are Knowledge vs unqualified Belief, the J T cell is the only one that can be marked off. J ¬T, ¬J T and ¬J ¬T all have to be called mere Belief. That makes Belief heterogeneous.

1. Justification without truth is lost. A justified false belief is epistemically good in the sense of being responsibly held, but not Knowledge because ¬T. On a binary taxonomy it must be called Belief and is lumped with unjustified false belief. Justification becomes invisible in the false domain; we cannot mark the normative difference between a rational error and an irrational error.

2. Truth without justification is lost. An unjustified true belief is true but held by luck/accident, not Knowledge because ¬J. On a binary taxonomy it must be called Belief and is lumped with justified false belief and with plain false belief. Truth becomes invisible in the non-knowledge domain; a lucky hit is epistemically indistinguishable from a false belief.

Hence JTB needs distinct intermediate states – justified belief and true belief – to keep justification and truth separately trackable. With only Knowledge/Belief the 2×2 J×T space collapses to two cells.

A second strand, Colleagues 1,13,14,9,5,7, and partly Colleague 2 and 6, frames the cost as justificatory regress / foundation. Because justification must be realized by a further epistemic state, on a Knowledge/Belief only inventory it must be a further belief or a piece of knowledge. Knowledge already requires justification, so a justifier that is knowledge reintroduces the same requirement. This yields Agrippa’s trilemma: infinite regress of justifiers Bq, Br, …; vicious circularity; or a dogmatic stopping point. A basic belief would be a Belief not justified by anything further, i.e. not Knowledge, so the chain rests on an arbitrary/unjustified foundation. Colleague 5 adds the basing-relation problem: JTB cannot explain why the belief is based on its justifier rather than merely coinciding with it using only K/B.

The two strands overlap: the regress/foundation worry is why a binary inventory cannot give justification an independent standing; the taxonomy worry is the observable consequence that JFB and UTB have no home and are conflated under mere Belief. The question explicitly limits epistemic states to Knowledge and Belief and asks to ignore Gettier, which points to the collapse of JFB and UTB as the direct binary-taxonomy problems, while regress/foundation is the classic structural cost of building justification out of belief/knowledge alone. Unresolved is whether the intended “two problems” are the two collapsed cells or regress + arbitrary foundation.

reflection_text.6:
The JTB analysis is K p ≡ B p ∧ T p ∧ J p. With only the two doxastic labels Knowledge and unqualified Belief there is no independent attitude for justification or for truth. The 2×2 justification × truth space therefore collapses to two cells:

* J ∧ T ∧ B = Knowledge
* ¬J ∧ T ∧ B , J ∧ ¬T ∧ B , ¬J ∧ ¬T ∧ B = all labelled Belief

That collapse is the core non-Gettier cost.

Two distinct non-knowledge positions are thereby lost inside the undifferentiated Belief bucket:

1. Justification without truth – justified false belief, J ∧ B ∧ ¬T. It is epistemically good in the sense of being responsibly held, but it is not Knowledge because ¬T. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it must be called mere Belief and is lumped together with unjustified false belief. Justification becomes invisible in the false domain; a rational error cannot be distinguished from an irrational error.

2. Truth without justification – unjustified true belief, T ∧ B ∧ ¬J. It is true but held by luck/accident and is not Knowledge because ¬J. On a Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it must also be called mere Belief and is lumped together with justified false belief and unjustified false belief. Truth becomes invisible in the non-knowledge domain; a lucky hit cannot be distinguished from a false belief.

Colleagues 10,11,12,3,4,6,8,2 phrase this as the heterogeneous catch-all Belief = JFB ∨ UTB ∨ UFB, loss of justified belief and true belief as intermediate states, and the inability to mark justification and truth as independent epistemic values.

A second, structurally related line of argument is raised by colleagues 1,13,14,9,2,5,6. Because J p can only be realised as K q or B q when only K and B are available, justification must be provided by another belief/knowledge. That yields the familiar Agrippa trilemma: an infinite regress of justifying beliefs K p → K q → K r…, a vicious circle, or a dogmatic stopping point where a basic belief is accepted without further justification. The stopping point can only be a mere Belief under the binary taxonomy, so it is not Knowledge and the regress either never terminates or terminates in an arbitrary, unjustified foundation. Colleague 5 additionally notes the basing-relation problem; colleague 7 notes an access/factivity worry.

I am keeping both descriptions in mind: the taxonomy collapse into JFB and UTB as the explicit two-cell loss, and the regress/arbitrary foundation formulation as the dynamic consequence of having to build justification out of only K and B. Unresolved is whether the intended “two problems” are meant as the two taxonomy conflations JFB and UTB, or as regress vs foundational arbitrariness. The discussion so far points to the former as the most directly tied to the Knowledge/Belief only restriction, with regress/foundation as its structural expression.

reflection_text.12:
The question is about the cost of a binary Knowledge / Belief ontology for a JTB analysis, ignoring Gettier.

Consensus across most colleagues is that with only K and B as tags the 2×2 justification × truth space collapses to two cells: T&J&B = Knowledge, everything else = unqualified Belief. That makes Belief a heterogeneous catch-all.

The two distinct non-knowledge positions that are lost are:

* J & B & ~T : justified false belief. Epistemically good in virtue of justification but false, so by JTB it is not Knowledge. On a K/B only taxonomy it must be called mere Belief and is therefore lumped with unjustified false belief. Justification is invisible in the false domain; a responsibly held error is epistemically indistinguishable from an irrational false belief.

* T & B & ~J : unjustified true belief / lucky true belief. True but held without good grounds, so by JTB it is not Knowledge. On a K/B only taxonomy it must also be called mere Belief and is therefore lumped with justified false belief and with unjustified false belief. Truth is invisible in the non-knowledge domain; a lucky hit is epistemically indistinguishable from a false belief.

Hence JTB needs distinct intermediate states – justified belief and true belief – to keep justification and truth separately trackable. With only K/B these are lost, Belief = JFB ∨ UTB ∨ UFB.

A second framing of the same pressure is expressed by colleagues 1,2,6,13,14 as the Agrippa trilemma/regress problem. If justification must be provided by an epistemic state, the justifier is itself a belief, and if that justifier must itself be justified the chain never terminates: infinite regress of justifiers, vicious circularity, or a dogmatic foundational stopping point that is merely Belief, not Knowledge. That is the regress/arbitrary foundation version of the collapse, and it is tied to the fact that there is no distinct ‘justified belief’ state to serve as a non-knowledge stopping point.

Disagreement / nuance noted: Colleague 5 and 7 also raise basing/access/factivity problems as a second structural difficulty; colleagues 1/13/14 present regress + arbitrary foundation as the two problems rather than the two mixed cases. The taxonomy collapse and the regress/foundation difficulty are presented by Colleague 2 and 6 as two sides of the same binary-ontology cost.

Unresolved for me: whether the exam wants the taxonomy collapse as two separate mixed cases – justified false belief vs unjustified true belief – or wants the classic regress/ foundation pair. The condition “only epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief” points strongly to the heterogeneity/collapse formulation, which also entails the regress problem.
reflection_text.11:
The question is about the cost of restricting the epistemic ontology to Knowledge and Belief under JTB = J & T & B.

Two clusters of replies emerged in round 0.

Taxonomic-collapse cluster. Colleagues 10,11,12,3,4,8 stress the 2×2 justification × truth space:
* J T B = Knowledge
* J F B = justified false belief
* U T B = unjustified true belief
* U F B = unjustified false belief

With only Knowledge / Belief as labels, the three non-K cells are forced into the single label ‘Belief’. Hence Belief becomes a heterogeneous catch-all.

1. Justification without truth is invisible. JFB is epistemically good in being justified but ¬T so by JTB it is not Knowledge. On a binary taxonomy it must be called mere Belief, and so it is lumped with UFB and with UTB. No distinct state for justified belief is available, so the normative value of justification is lost in the false domain. Relatedly, if belief is defined as non-knowledge, justified false belief becomes impossible or is misclassified as knowledge.

2. Truth without justification is invisible. UTB is true but ¬J so by JTB it is not Knowledge. On a binary taxonomy it must be called mere Belief, and so it is lumped with JFB and UFB. No distinct state for true belief is available, so the normative difference between a lucky true hit and a responsible true belief is lost; truth is invisible in the non-knowledge domain.

In effect JTB can only register justification when truth is present and only register truth when justification is present. The classic intermediate categories justified belief and true belief have no home.

Regress/foundation cluster. Colleagues 1,13,14,9,2,6,5,7 argue the binary ontology forces justification to be reconstrued as belief/knowledge. A justifier for p must be a belief q or a knowledge q. If it is a belief it needs its own justification, etc. That yields:
* infinite regress of justifiers: B p justified by B q justified by B r...
* no non-arbitrary stopping point: a basic belief would be a belief justified without further justification, i.e. a mere Belief not Knowledge, so the chain rests on dogmatic/arbitrary foundation. Some formulations add circularity/vicious self-justification, basing-relation gap, or access/factivity problems.

Disagreement / overlap. The regress argument is a general JTB problem and is made acute by the Knowledge/Belief restriction because there is no third ‘justified belief’ attitude to stop in. Colleagues 2 and 6 note both the regress/circularity structure and the taxonomic collapse. Colleague 5 frames the second problem as the basing relation; colleague 7 as access/factivity.

Current take. The condition “only epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief” most directly licenses the taxonomic collapse: JFB and UTB are the two epistemically distinct non-knowledge positions that JTB forces into an undifferentiated Belief bucket. The regress/foundation difficulty is a related structural consequence of having no independent justification attitude, and remains a live contender in the discussion. Unresolved whether the intended “two problems” are the pair JFB / UTB collapse or regress + arbitrary foundation; the literature often treats them together. Gettier is explicitly to be ignored.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think we can consolidate several of the threads. If Knowledge and Belief are the only epistemic states, justification cannot be an independent state. So any justifier has to be either another belief or a piece of knowledge. If it is a belief, it needs a further justifier; if it is knowledge, it already requires justification, so it cannot ground the original belief without moving the problem up a level. That gives the first structural problem: the infinite regress/termination failure of justification. I would treat circularity as the looped variant of this same failure, not as a separate second problem, unless we are listing all Agrippa horns rather than the two JTB-specific issues here.

The second distinct problem is the one colleagues 3, 4, 8, 10, 11, and 12 have been pressing: the K/B taxonomy collapses. JTB needs truth and justification to be separately trackable, but with only Knowledge and Belief every non-JTB case is dumped into “Belief.” So justified false belief and unjustified true belief become indistinguishable from ordinary unjustified false belief. That is not a Gettier issue; it is a pre-Gettier expressive failure of the two-state scheme.

So the two problems I’d put in the final answer are: (1) infinite regress of justification, and (2) collapse of the Knowledge/Belief taxonomy, where justified false beliefs and lucky true beliefs have no distinct category. This integrates the regress thread and the taxonomy thread and avoids multiplying separate horns.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: With a strict Knowledge / Belief binary JTB can only mark the conjunction J & T & B.

On the JTB matrix of justification x truth x belief you have in principle

* J & T & B = Knowledge
* J & ~T & B = justified false belief
* ~J & T & B = unjustified true / lucky true belief
* ~J & ~T & B = unjustified false belief

If the only predicates you are allowed to use are Knowledge and unqualified Belief the first cell is Knowledge and the remaining three cells are all forced into the single label ‘Belief’. Belief becomes a heterogeneous catch-all and justification and truth can only be registered together.

1. Justification is invisible in the false domain. JTB entails justified false beliefs. A justified false belief is epistemically good in being responsibly held but ~T so it is not Knowledge. On a K/B only taxonomy it must be called mere Belief and is therefore indistinguishable from an unjustified false belief. You lose the ability to mark the normative difference between a rational error and an irrational error, i.e. you have no distinct state of justified belief. Justification only “counts” when truth is present.

2. Truth is invisible in the non-knowledge domain. JTB entails true beliefs that are not justified. An unjustified true belief is true but held by luck/accident, ~J so it is not Knowledge. On a K/B only taxonomy it must also be called mere Belief and is therefore indistinguishable from justified false beliefs and from false beliefs generally. You lose the ability to mark the normative difference between a lucky hit and a justified error, i.e. you have no distinct state of true belief. Truth only “counts” when justification is present.

Hence with only Knowledge and Belief JFB and UTB have no home. The classic intermediate states justified belief and true belief are needed to keep justification and truth trackable independently of their conjunction. This is the pre-Gettier taxonomic cost of the binary ontology, distinct from the regress/foundation Agrippa problem that is also raised in the room.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’d narrow the answer to the justificatory structure itself. The taxonomy worries are real, but they seem downstream: they arise because justification is not an independent epistemic state, and that same defect generates the classic justificatory problem. If Knowledge and Belief are the only available states, then a justifier for p must be either another Knowledge or another Belief. If it is Knowledge, it must itself be justified; if it is Belief, it still needs justification to do any work. So we get an endless demand for further justifiers. The only way to stop is to posit some belief accepted without further epistemic support. But under the K/B inventory that stopping point is just Belief, not Knowledge—or else it is already justified Knowledge, which simply restarts the demand. So the two problems are (1) infinite regress of justification and (2) the arbitrary/unjustified stopping point or foundation.

I’d resist treating circularity as a separate second item here. In the Agrippa trilemma it is usually listed alongside regress and dogmatic stopping, but in this specific JTB/K-B setting it does not give an independent resolution. A circle of mutually supporting beliefs either continues the same regress around a loop or must be cut off by treating one member as basic, which is precisely the arbitrary-foundation problem. So the clean two-problem formulation is infinite regress plus arbitrary termination.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: At this point I think the strongest line is to separate the core justificatory structure from the taxonomy complaints. The taxonomy-collapse points are real, but they are downstream of the fact that, with only Knowledge and Belief, there is no independent category of justified belief. So any justifier has to be either another belief or a piece of knowledge. If it is a belief, it needs its own justification, and we get an infinite regress. If it is knowledge, its justificatory status is already part of what needs grounding, so it either restarts the same demand at a higher level or turns into a loop.

The crucial dilemma is where the chain stops. Under JTB plus only Knowledge/Belief, it cannot stop at a justified basic belief, because such a stopping point would be neither Knowledge nor a distinct justified-belief state—it would just be mere Belief. So the chain either never terminates or terminates arbitrarily in something unjustified/dogmatic. That gives the two core problems as (1) the infinite regress of justification and (2) the arbitrary or dogmatic stopping point / foundationalist dilemma.

I would not treat circularity as a separate second problem here. It is better seen as a degenerate form of the same failure: a closed loop is just a regress that never reaches an independent justifier. The Agrippa-style options are regress, circularity, and arbitrary stopping point, but under the binary Knowledge/Belief constraint the sharp two-part problem is endless regress versus an unjustified stopping place. Gettier cases aside, that seems to be the structural difficulty JTB runs into.

3.text:
With JTB the logical space is J × T × B. On the usual reading B is presupposed, so the interesting
space is the 2×2 J×T space.

* J T = justified true belief = Knowledge on JTB
* J ¬T = justified false belief
* ¬J T = unjustified true belief / lucky true belief
* ¬J ¬T = unjustified false belief

If the only ascriptions you are allowed to make are *knows that p* and *believes that p* the J T cell
is the only one that can be marked off as a distinct kind. The other three cells are all forced
into the undifferentiated residual category ‘mere Belief’. Belief therefore becomes an
unprincipled heterogeneous catch-all.

That collapse has two sides.

1. Justification without truth is invisible. A justified false belief is epistemically good
in the sense of being responsibly held, and it is not Knowledge because ¬T. On a
Knowledge/Belief only taxonomy it has to be called Belief and is lumped together with
unjustified false belief and with ¬J T. So the normative difference between a rational
error and an irrational error cannot be marked. Justification can only be registered
when truth is also present; justification as an independent epistemic value is lost in
the false domain.

2. Truth without justification is invisible. An unjustified true belief is true but held
by luck/accident, and it is not Knowledge because ¬J. On a Knowledge/Belief only
taxonomy it has to be called Belief and is lumped together with justified false belief
and with plain false belief. So the normative difference between a lucky hit and a
genuinely supported error cannot be marked. Truth as an independent epistemic value
is lost in the non-knowledge domain.

Hence with only Knowledge vs Belief JTB cannot keep the four JTB cells distinct:
justified belief, i.e. JFB, and true belief, i.e. UTB, have no home. That is the
pre-Gettier taxonomic cost of reducing knowledge to a species of belief. It is the
doxastic counterpart of the familiar regress/foundation worry: because justification
has no independent attitude status it must be realised by a further belief/knowledge,
which is why the J¬T and ¬JT cells cannot be named.

4.text:
With only the predicates *knows that p* and *believes that p* the three-place conjunction J∧T∧B can be marked off once, everything else is forced into an undifferentiated Belief bucket.

Knowledge on JTB = B ∧ T ∧ J

Hence on a K/B inventory the 2×2 justification × truth space is reduced to

* T ∧ J ∧ B = Knowledge
* ~T ∧ J ∧ B , T ∧ ~J ∧ B , ~T ∧ ~J ∧ B = Belief

Belief is therefore a heterogeneous disjunction and justification and truth can only be registered together.

1. Justification without truth – justified false belief.
J ∧ B ∧ ~T is not Knowledge because ~T. With only Knowledge/Belief it must be classed as mere Belief. A justified false belief is epistemically good in the sense of being responsibly held, and it is a different error from an unjustified false belief. On the binary taxonomy both are just ‘Belief’. Justification is invisible in the false domain; you lose a distinct state of justified belief and the normative difference between a rationally held false belief and an irrationally held false belief cannot be marked.

2. Truth without justification – unjustified true belief.
T ∧ B ∧ ~J is not Knowledge because ~J. With only Knowledge/Belief it must be classed as mere Belief. An unjustified true belief is a lucky hit, epistemically defective, and it is a different case from a justified false belief. On the binary taxonomy both are just ‘Belief’. Truth is invisible in the non-knowledge domain; you lose a distinct state of true belief and the normative difference between a lucky true belief and a false belief, justified or not, cannot be marked.

In effect JTB can only register justification when truth is present and can only register truth when justification is present. Justified false belief and unjustified true belief have no distinct epistemic place and are both downgraded to unqualified Belief. That is the pre-Gettier taxonomic cost of trying to build justification out of the Knowledge/Belief divide alone, and it is what drives the familiar Agrippa regress/foundation worry once justification is reconstrued as further beliefs/knowledge.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the cleanest answer is the taxonomy-collapse one, and I’d resist treating the Agrippa regress as the central pair here. Regress/circularity is a general problem for any theory that demands justification; it arises only once one assumes every justifier must itself be justified. But the question’s special constraint is narrower and more damaging: if the only available epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief, then JTB cannot keep justification and truth as independent conditions. That yields two distinct problems:

1. Justified false belief. JTB entails that a belief can be justified yet false. Such a belief is not Knowledge, so on a K/B-only taxonomy it must fall into mere Belief. But so does unjustified false belief. Thus justification is invisible in the false case; a responsibly held error is classified exactly like a random false belief.

2. Unjustified true belief. JTB entails that a belief can be true yet unjustified—a lucky guess, wishful thinking, etc. It is not Knowledge, so it too must fall into mere Belief. But so does false belief. Thus truth is invisible in the non-knowledge case; a lucky true belief is classified exactly like a false belief.

So JTB’s own three conditions collapse: the only positive cell is J&T&B = Knowledge, and all other combinations are an undifferentiated Belief. The regress or circularity can be a downstream consequence of trying to make justification another K/B item, but it is not one of the two direct JTB problems under the stated K/B-only taxonomy. The two problems are the loss of justified false belief as a distinct status and the loss of unjustified true belief as a distinct status. That is why colleagues 3, 4, 8, 10, 11, and 12 have the right diagnosis.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the discussion has isolated the right first problem but is beginning to double-count the second. The unavoidable first problem is the regress of justification: if justification must be cashed out using only Knowledge and Belief, then each justifier is either another belief needing support or an already-known belief whose own justification is again in question. Circularity is important here, but it should not be treated as a separate problem. A circle of beliefs justifying each other is simply the regress that loops rather than continues; it is one horn of the same Agrippa-style dilemma, not an additional structural cost.

The second distinct problem is the collapse of the Knowledge/Belief taxonomy. On JTB, Knowledge = Justified & True & Belief. If everything that is not Knowledge must be mere Belief, then justified false belief, unjustified true belief, and unjustified false belief all occupy one undifferentiated category. Justification becomes invisible when truth fails, and truth becomes invisible when justification fails. This is independent of how we handle the regress: even if we somehow stop the justificatory chain, the K/B-only framework still cannot represent the difference between a well-supported error and a lucky true guess. So I would frame the two problems as (1) the regress of justification and (2) the collapse of the Knowledge/Belief taxonomy, with circularity treated as a variant of the regress rather than a separate second problem.

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the discussion is splitting because several items are being treated as separate problems when they are really one horn of the same difficulty. Under JTB, \(Kp \iff Bp \land Tp \land Jp\). If the only epistemic states available are Knowledge and Belief, then \(Jp\) cannot be a primitive third state. Any justifier must be either a further belief or a piece of knowledge; and since knowledge itself includes justified belief, even a K-justifier just reintroduces the need for justification. That gives the justificatory-chain problem: an endless regress, or a loop/circle, or an arbitrary stopping point. But circularity and arbitrary foundations are not independent second problems; they are alternative ways the same regress horn fails to terminate non-arbitrarily.

The genuinely distinct second problem is the collapse of the Knowledge/Belief taxonomy. JTB requires truth and justification to remain independently trackable. With only K and B, however, the space collapses: \(T \land J\) is Knowledge, while \(J \land \neg T\), \(\neg J \land T\), and \(\neg J \land \neg T\) are all just “Belief.” So justified false belief and unjustified true belief lose their distinct status. That is not just another version of the regress; it is the representational inadequacy of a binary K/B ontology for a tripartite JTB analysis.

So I would frame the two non-Gettier problems as: (1) infinite regress of justification, with circularity and arbitrary stopping points as subcases of that failure; and (2) collapse of the K/B taxonomy into an undifferentiated catch-all Belief. Counting circularity as a separate second problem risks double-counting one justificatory-chain issue and missing the independent taxonomy problem.

11.text:
With only Knowledge = J & T & B and the residual category Belief = not Knowledge, the J x T space cannot be marked independently of the Knowledge/ Belief divide.

The JTB analysis generates four doxastic positions with respect to p:

* J T B = Knowledge
* J ¬T B = justified false belief
* ¬J T B = unjustified true belief
* ¬J ¬T B = unjustified false belief

On a strict Knowledge/Belief ontology the last three are all forced into the single label ‘Belief’. Belief therefore becomes a heterogeneous catch-all and two epistemically distinct non-knowledge positions disappear.

1. Justification without truth is invisible. J & B & ¬T is a justified false belief. It is epistemically good in the sense of being responsibly held, but ¬T so by JTB it is not Knowledge. On a binary taxonomy it must be called mere Belief and is lumped together with ¬J ¬T B and ¬J T B. There is no way to mark the normative value of justification in the false domain; a carefully justified error is indistinguishable from an irrational false belief, and in the limit belief is defined as unjustified so justified false belief has no home at all.

On a binary taxonomy it must also be called mere Belief and is lumped together with J ¬T B and ¬J ¬T B. There is no way to mark the normative defect of luck in the true domain; a lucky true belief is indistinguishable from a false belief and from a justified false belief.

Hence JTB can only register justification when truth is present and can only register truth when justification is present. The classic intermediate states justified belief and true belief have no distinct place. That is the taxonomic price of reducing the epistemic ontology to Knowledge vs Belief. The regress/ foundation difficulty is the structural consequence of this collapse: with no independent ‘justified belief’ attitude, a justifier must be reconstrued as a further belief or a piece of knowledge, which drives the familiar Agrippa trilemma.

reconstrued as another belief, giving the Agrippa trilemma of infinite

With the JTB analysis

K p  iff  B p & T p & J p

the justification × truth matrix has four distinct doxastic positions in the belief domain

* J & T = Knowledge
* J & ¬T = justified false belief
* ¬J & T = unjustified / lucky true belief
* ¬J & ¬T = unjustified false belief

If Knowledge and unqualified Belief are the only attitude predicates that are available, the J & T cell is the only one that can be marked off as distinct. Everything else is forced into the single label ‘Belief’.

That makes Belief a heterogeneous catch-all and it removes justification and truth as independently trackable epistemic values outside Knowledge.

1. Justification without truth is invisible. J & B & ¬T is not Knowledge because ¬T and with only K/B it must be called Belief. A responsibly held error is therefore lumped together with ¬J & B & ¬T and with ¬J & B & T. Justification can be marked only when truth is present. In effect there is no distinct state of justified belief: a justified false belief is epistemically better than an unjustified false belief, but the taxonomy cannot mark the difference, and on a strict K/B inventory justification is invisible in the false domain.

2. Truth without justification is invisible. ¬J & B & T is not Knowledge because ¬J and with only K/B it must be called Belief. A lucky hit is therefore lumped together with J & B & ¬T and with ¬J & B & ¬T. Truth can be marked only when justification is present. In effect there is no distinct state of true belief / accidental belief: an unjustified true belief is epistemically defective in being lucky, but the taxonomy cannot distinguish it from a justified false belief, and truth is invisible in the non-knowledge domain.

Hence on a K/B only ontology JFB and UTB have no home. The familiar talk of a distinct justified belief and a distinct true belief is lost and Belief = JFB ∨ UTB ∨ UFB. That is the formal taxonomic cost of reducing justification to the knowledge/belief divide. It is the same point that is usually expressed in regress terms: with no third attitude for justification, J p must be reconstrued as B q or K q, so a justifier either generates an endless chain of justifying beliefs or must stop in an unjustified, i.e. merely believed, basic; justification cannot be given an independent epistemic home without either regress or an arbitrary dogmatic foundation.

I think we can consolidate several of the threads. If Knowledge and Belief are the only epistemic states, justification cannot be an independent state. So any justifier has to be either another belief or a piece of knowledge. If it is a belief, it needs a further justifier; if it is knowledge, it already requires justification, so it cannot ground the original belief without moving the problem up a level. That gives the first structural problem: the infinite regress/termination failure of justification. I would treat circularity as the looped variant of this same failure, not as a separate second problem, unless we are listing all Agrippa horns rather than the two JTB-specific issues here.

The second distinct problem is the one colleagues 3, 4, 8, 10, 11, and 12 have been pressing: the K/B taxonomy collapses. JTB needs truth and justification to be separately trackable, but with only Knowledge and Belief every non-JTB case is dumped into “Belief.” So justified false belief and unjustified true belief become indistinguishable from ordinary unjustified false belief. That is not a Gettier issue; it is a pre-Gettier expressive failure of the two-state scheme.

So the two problems I’d put in the final answer are: (1) infinite regress of justification, and (2) collapse of the Knowledge/Belief taxonomy, where justified false beliefs and lucky true beliefs have no distinct category. This integrates the regress thread and the taxonomy thread and avoids multiplying separate horns.

With a strict Knowledge / Belief binary JTB can only mark the conjunction J & T & B.

On the JTB matrix of justification x truth x belief you have in principle

* J & T & B = Knowledge
* J & ~T & B = justified false belief
* ~J & T & B = unjustified true / lucky true belief
* ~J & ~T & B = unjustified false belief

If the only predicates you are allowed to use are Knowledge and unqualified Belief the first cell is Knowledge and the remaining three cells are all forced into the single label ‘Belief’. Belief becomes a heterogeneous catch-all and justification and truth can only be registered together.

On a K/B only taxonomy it must be called mere Belief and is therefore indistinguishable from an unjustified false belief. You lose the ability to mark the normative difference between a rational error and an irrational error, i.e. you have no distinct state of justified belief. Justification only “counts” when truth is present.

2. Truth is invisible in the non-knowledge domain. JTB entails true beliefs that are not justified. An unjustified true belief is true but held by luck/accident, ~J so it is not Knowledge. On a K/B only taxonomy it must also be called mere Belief and is therefore indistinguishable from justified false beliefs and from false beliefs generally. You lose the ability to mark the normative difference between a lucky hit and a justified error, i.e. you have no distinct state of true belief. Truth only “counts” when justification is present.

The classic intermediate states justified belief and true belief are needed to keep justification and truth trackable independently of their conjunction. public_text.7:
I’d narrow the answer to the justificatory structure itself. The taxonomy worries are real, but they seem downstream: they arise because justification is not an independent epistemic state, and that same defect generates the classic justificatory problem. If Knowledge and Belief are the only available states, then a justifier for p must be either another Knowledge or another Belief. If it is Knowledge, it must itself be justified; if it is Belief, it still needs justification to do any work. So we get an endless demand for further justifiers. The only way to stop is to posit some belief accepted without further epistemic support. But under the K/B inventory that stopping point is just Belief, not Knowledge—or else it is already justified Knowledge, which simply restarts the demand. So the two problems are (1) infinite regress of justification and (2) the arbitrary/unjustified stopping point or foundation.

I’d resist treating circularity as a separate second item here. In the Agrippa trilemma it is usually listed alongside regress and dogmatic stopping, but in this specific JTB/K-B setting it does not give an independent resolution. A circle of mutually supporting beliefs either continues the same regress around a loop or must be cut off by treating one member as basic, which is precisely the arbitrary-foundation problem. So the clean two-problem formulation is infinite regress plus arbitrary termination.
public_text.5:
At this point I think the strongest line is to separate the core justificatory structure from the taxonomy complaints. The taxonomy-collapse points are real, but they are downstream of the fact that, with only Knowledge and Belief, there is no independent category of justified belief. So any justifier has to be either another belief or a piece of knowledge. If it is a belief, it needs its own justification, and we get an infinite regress. If it is knowledge, its justificatory status is already part of what needs grounding, so it either restarts the same demand at a higher level or turns into a loop.

The crucial dilemma is where the chain stops. Under JTB plus only Knowledge/Belief, it cannot stop at a justified basic belief, because such a stopping point would be neither Knowledge nor a distinct justified-belief state—it would just be mere Belief. So the chain either never terminates or terminates arbitrarily in something unjustified/dogmatic. That gives the two core problems as (1) the infinite regress of justification and (2) the arbitrary or dogmatic stopping point / foundationalist dilemma.

I would not treat circularity as a separate second problem here. It is better seen as a degenerate form of the same failure: a closed loop is just a regress that never reaches an independent justifier. The Agrippa-style options are regress, circularity, and arbitrary stopping point, but under the binary Knowledge/Belief constraint the sharp two-part problem is endless regress versus an unjustified stopping place. Gettier cases aside, that seems to be the structural difficulty JTB runs into.
